evals.name: rough-notes-to-full-spec
evals.prompt:
I've got some rough notes for a feature on my side project (a recipe-sharing web app). Turn them into a proper spec document and save it as spec.md.

Notes:
"Want to add meal-plan export. Users can export their weekly meal plan, probably PDF, maybe also CSV? Should be fast and look nice. Premium users only I think. Need to handle big plans somehow, and probably rate limit it so people don't hammer the server. Also localisation at some point."
evals.expected_output: A structured spec with narrative problem/summary sections, EARS-shaped requirements each carrying exactly one capitalized RFC 2119 keyword, Gherkin acceptance criteria, an explicit out-of-scope section, and undecided points (PDF vs CSV, 'big plans', 'at some point') surfaced as open questions rather than silently decided.
assertions: Requirements follow an EARS shape: ubiquitous, When (event), While (state), If...then (unwanted), or Where (optional feature), each with a named system as actor
Each requirement contains exactly one capitalized RFC 2119 keyword (MUST/MUST NOT/SHOULD/SHOULD NOT/MAY)
Undecided points from the notes (CSV yes/no, what counts as a 'big plan', localisation timing) are surfaced as explicit open questions or out-of-scope items, not silently decided
The vague qualities 'fast' and 'look nice' are quantified with measurable targets or raised as open questions — the bare adjectives do not appear inside requirements
The spec contains an explicit out-of-scope / no-gos section
Requirements have Given/When/Then acceptance scenarios describing observable behaviour

evals.name: tighten-vague-requirements
evals.prompt:
Here's the requirements section from our internal PRD for a webhook delivery service. My team lead says it's "too vague to build against". Rewrite it so it's unambiguous and testable, and save the result as requirements.md.

- The system should deliver webhooks quickly and reliably.
- Failed webhooks should be retried as appropriate.
- The dashboard should show relevant delivery stats.
- Webhooks must be secure.
- The system should handle a large number of events, etc.
evals.expected_output: Rewritten requirements with weak words (quickly, reliably, as appropriate, relevant, secure, large, etc.) eliminated in favour of measurable targets with units, one thought per requirement, active voice with a named actor, and invented numbers flagged as assumptions needing confirmation rather than presented as fact.
assertions: No weak words survive inside rewritten requirements: quickly, reliably, as appropriate, relevant, large, etc./and so on are all gone or replaced with measurable criteria
Performance, retry, and scale claims carry numbers with units (e.g. latency in ms, retry count/backoff schedule, events per second)
Each requirement expresses a single obligation — no 'and'/'or' joining two independent obligations in one statement
Numeric targets invented by the model are flagged as assumptions or questions for the team to confirm, not presented as settled fact
Requirements use active voice with a named actor and a capitalized RFC 2119 keyword (e.g. 'The delivery service MUST ...')

evals.name: ambiguity-trap-slack-thread
evals.prompt:
Turn this Slack thread into a spec for our note-taking app's offline mode feature. Save it as offline-spec.md.

jake: we should let people use the app offline
me: yeah, at least viewing. editing offline is trickier — conflicts
jake: maybe last-write-wins? or we could block editing entirely
me: not sure. also how much do we cache? everything seems like a lot
jake: whatever's easiest
evals.expected_output: A spec whose requirements cover only the decided scope (offline viewing), with the conflict-resolution strategy (last-write-wins vs block editing) and cache scope surfaced as explicit open questions with options — NOT silently resolved by the model picking an answer.
assertions: The conflict-resolution choice (last-write-wins vs block offline editing) appears as an explicit open question with the options laid out — the spec does not silently pick one
Cache scope ('how much do we cache') is surfaced as an open question or explicit decision-needed item, not silently decided
Normative requirements only cover the decided scope (offline viewing); no requirement commits the product to a specific conflict strategy
Requirements that do exist are testable: capitalized modal keyword, named actor, observable behaviour
